name: Colin Whitmore
presenting_complaint: Ward referral: creatinine risen from 92 to 188 micromol/L with reduced urine output

medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily (for back pain)
Recent contrast CT chest on admission

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: You are called to review a 74-year-old man on day 3 of an admission for pneumonia. His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 92 to 188 micromol/L and urine output has fallen to under 0.5 mL/kg/hr over the last 8 hours. He is on perindopril, ibuprofen and gentamicin, and had a contrast CT on admission. Obs: BP 104/62, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 96%, temp 37.1, GCS 15.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the reviewing RMO.

subjective: Establish baseline renal function and timeline of the creatinine rise and urine output fall
Screen for pre-renal causes: fluid intake, vomiting/diarrhoea, sepsis, poor oral intake, symptoms of hypovolaemia or heart failure
Screen for post-renal (obstructive) symptoms: known BPH, difficulty voiding, suprapubic discomfort, catheter status
Review the DRUG CHART for nephrotoxics: NSAID (ibuprofen), ACE inhibitor (perindopril), gentamicin, and recent iodinated contrast
Ask about symptoms suggesting intrinsic renal disease: rash, arthralgia, haematuria (glomerulonephritis/interstitial nephritis), muscle pain (rhabdomyolysis)
objective: Clinical assessment of fluid status: JVP, mucous membranes, skin turgor, peripheral oedema, capillary refill, lying/standing BP
BLADDER SCAN and post-void residual to exclude obstruction; palpate for a distended bladder
Review fluid balance chart, daily weights, drug chart, recent contrast exposure and sepsis markers
Bloods: UEC/creatinine (stage by KDIGO), FBC, CRP, VBG for acid-base, and urgent POTASSIUM given AKI; urinalysis (blood/protein) and gentamicin level
12-lead ECG if hyperkalaemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS); arrange renal tract ultrasound if obstruction not excluded on bladder scan
assessment: Acute kidney injury on the ward — classify as pre-renal, intrinsic (renal) or post-renal
Most likely multifactorial: nephrotoxic drugs (ibuprofen, ACE inhibitor, gentamicin, contrast) plus possible pre-renal hypovolaemia/sepsis from pneumonia
Stage severity by KDIGO (creatinine rise and urine output); exclude post-renal obstruction (BPH)
plan: Classify the AKI out loud as pre-renal / renal / post-renal and stage by KDIGO (FIRST step)
STOP nephrotoxics immediately: cease ibuprofen (NSAID), withhold perindopril (ACE inhibitor), stop/hold gentamicin and review level, and avoid further iodinated contrast
RE-DOSE the entire drug chart for renal function — do NOT leave medications at pre-AKI doses; adjust or withhold renally-cleared/nephrotoxic agents per eTG/renal guidance
Assess and correct fluid status: careful IV fluid replacement if pre-renal/hypovolaemic; treat underlying sepsis (pneumonia) appropriately
Exclude obstruction: bladder scan +/- catheter; arrange renal tract ultrasound if residual high or cause unclear
Monitor potassium and acid-base with serial VBG/UEC; treat hyperkalaemia if present (calcium, insulin-dextrose, salbutamol)
Strict fluid balance chart, urinary catheter for hourly output, and daily weights
Know dialysis indications (AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia) and escalate to renal/medical registrar if refractory or worsening

critical_errors: Leaving the drug chart at pre-AKI doses and failing to stop nephrotoxics (ibuprofen, perindopril, gentamicin) or account for recent contrast — continuing to injure the kidney
Not seeking the cause by category (pre-renal / renal / post-renal), so a reversible cause such as bladder outlet obstruction (BPH) is missed
Failing to check and monitor potassium, missing dangerous AKI-associated hyperkalaemia
must_not_miss: Post-renal obstruction (BPH) excluded with a bladder scan
Nephrotoxic drugs stopped and the whole drug chart re-dosed for renal function
